# Brief: an image subtitle read that runs out of time (JS-089)

**Situation today (before JS-089).** When a viewer seeks to a point where an image subtitle (PGS) cue began long before, the server reads the film from where that cue began, so the picture can show it. The longer ago the cue began, the more of the film is read, so such a seek is slower and costs more reads than an ordinary one.

**After JS-089.** The first play of a film starts a background read that copies its image subtitle tracks into a small store. Seeks then read the stored track, and every seek costs the same. The background read has a fixed limit of one hour. A film is read at the speed of its store, so a 40 GB film needs about 11 MB/s to finish within the hour.

**The question.** A film whose read does not finish within the hour: what then?

**Options:**
1. **Retry on every play** (the build's first behaviour). Each play of that film starts another hour of reading. If the store is too slow for one hour, it is too slow every time, so the library is read again and again: up to an hour of store reads per play, for nothing.
2. **Remember the failure** (the build now). It is retried about once a day, at most an hour of reads a day, or at once if the file changes. The viewer still gets the subtitle drawn as before JS-089. Only that film's seeks into long cues stay as slow as today, until a retry succeeds.
3. **A limit that grows with the file's size**, for example the hour scaled to a minimum speed. More films finish, but a very slow store could still keep a large film reading for hours. Not built; a follow-up task.
4. **No limit.** Every film eventually finishes, but a store that hangs holds a worker slot (of 2 background slots per worker) indefinitely.

**Who is affected.** Only films too large for their store's speed: unverified how many. On the dogfood's store, a 40 GB film read in well under an hour (unverified figure).

**What the viewer loses with option 2:** for such a film, the JS-089 improvement (equal-cost seeks into long image cues) does not arrive. Nothing else changes from today. Logs tell the operator, and docs/running.md says what they can do (a faster store).

# Brief: JS-089's whole-film read when an image subtitle is first burned in

The owner has delegated this decision to you (2026-11-19). You escalated it from the time-limit brief (D-002).

**Today.** A viewer whose client cannot draw image subtitles (PGS, VobSub) gets them burned into the picture. The burn reads the subtitle's packets from the same read as the video, so it costs no extra network and no storage. A seek to a point where a cue began long before reads the film back from where that cue began: about 0.3 MB and 0.04 s per second of the cue's age, uncapped. docs/transcoding.md measures 2.78 s to the first segment for a cue 50 s old at 640x360, and more for a 4K film. The owner asked on 2026-11-12 for that cost to go (the task says "as text tracks are": each text track is already extracted once by reading the whole film).

**JS-089 as built.**
- The first time a play burns one of a film's image tracks, a background job reads the **whole film** once to copy its image tracks into the asset store: a few MB stored, but a 40 GB remux means 40 GB of media-store reads. This happens even if the viewer stops a minute later.
- The viewer does not wait for it. That is shown by a test in which no request of the play waits on the job.
- Every later seek into a long cue, by anyone, reads the small stored track: equal-cost seeks whatever the cue's age.
- It runs only when a burn of an image track is chosen, not on other plays. It runs once per film; how long the stored copy is kept is unverified.

**Who is affected, and how often.**
- Viewers of films with PGS or VobSub tracks whose client cannot draw them (for example jellyfin-web for PGS in some cases), who turn the subtitle on.
- The read happens once per such film, ever, plus the daily retry D-002 accepted for films that time out.
- How many films that is on the dogfood: unverified.
- On S3 the read is egress the operator pays for. A self-hosted store pays in disk and network time.

**Options.**
1. **Ship as built.** The cost is one whole-film read per film the first time its image subtitle is burned in, including for viewers who stop early. Every viewer after gets cheap seeks.
2. **Copy only when needed.** Start the copy on the first seek into a cue that began more than some threshold ago (say 30 s), or after the viewer has watched some minutes, so that a viewer who stops early, or never seeks, costs nothing. That first slow seek stays as slow as today; later ones are cheap. This needs a change to JS-089 and a check. Estimated at one more fix round (unverified).
3. **Defer JS-089.** Keep today's behaviour: no whole-film read, and seeks into long image cues cost more the older the cue.
4. **Keep the guarantee another way.** A design that learns where the image track's packets sit without reading the whole film (Matroska cue entries for the subtitle track, when the file has them) is not known to exist for the general case. Unverified; it would need a spike.

**Related.** PRODUCT.md line 59: "A transcode reads only as far ahead as the viewer needs, so a viewer who stops early doesn't cost the whole film's reading." DOMAINS 51 (in the JS-089 change) states the cost: "copying a PGS track reads the whole film from the media store once for each track of each film ... as extracting text does".

# Brief: counting subtitle work in the burn-in check (replay)

**Situation.** A viewer whose client cannot draw image subtitles (PGS, VobSub) gets them burned into the picture. A browser check for that behaviour (JS-071) plays such a film. It requires that no request of the play waits on subtitle extraction work, and asserts it by counting the subtitle jobs created during the play: the count must not grow.

**The change.** JS-089 (a seek into a long-showing image subtitle costs no more than any seek) adds a background job. The first time a film is played, a worker copies the film's image subtitle tracks into a store. Later seeks read the small stored track instead of reading the film from far back. The viewer does not wait for this job. It creates one new job row per film, so the check's count grows by one and the check fails.

**Kinds of subtitle job that exist:**
- `track`: a text track a viewer waits for;
- `fonts`: fonts for styled subtitles;
- `sup`: an image track a client draws itself;
- `chapters`: chapter pictures, background;
- `images`: the new one, background.

**Options:**
1. Stop counting `images`, `sup`, `fonts` and `chapters` jobs in the check, and count only `track`. This is simple, and the check passes.
2. Keep the check unchanged. JS-089 cannot ship as built.

**Who is affected.** Every viewer of a film with image subtitles whose client cannot draw them; on the dogfood library, most films with PGS tracks.

**Evidence.** The count grows by exactly one per first play (measured in the e2e run).


Lead's evidence (follow-up): 1. Built the narrow option: the check counts track, sup, fonts and chapters as before; only images is left out, and a second assertion requires the images count to grow by at most 1 per play. 2. A test plays through the real handlers (PlaybackInfo, both playlists, two replicas) with the images job held running: every request returns; a mutant that waits on the job fails it. Not covered then: the first segment. 3. The read cost is D-003. 4. A seek before the job finishes takes today's path at today's cost. 5. docs/subtitles.md:58 is being corrected to cite D-003.

# Brief: browser-engine clients and CORS (issue #202, from Fluster)

**Today.** A client whose interface runs in a browser engine fails before sign-in. That covers a web app served from another origin, and a desktop app built on a WebView, as Fluster is (Tauri). Two things block it:
- API responses carry no `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`, so the engine withholds them from the client, starting with `GET /System/Info/Public`.
- `OPTIONS` preflights answer 404, and the engine sends one before any request with an auth header or a JSON body.

Native clients (jellyfin-web served by jellyscale itself, Findroid, Swiftfin) are unaffected, because they do not enforce CORS or share the server's origin. **Fluster cannot connect to jellyscale at all** (the issue's repro). Per D-007, Fluster ships with jellyscale and ranks right after jellyfin-web.

**What Jellyfin 12.4 does** (as the issue reports it; not yet observed by jellyscale on a running 12.4: unverified):
- any origin allowed;
- preflights answered for every route, allowing the auth headers, `Content-Type` and `Range`;
- range headers exposed.

**Facts about jellyscale's authorization** (the lead checked these in the code):
- **No cookies.** A viewer's token travels only in a request header, or as an `ApiKey` query parameter on subtitle and font URLs inside playlists.
- So a page on another origin cannot make a viewer's browser send that viewer's token. A cross-origin page can only use a token it already holds. PRODUCT.md's authorization principle (nothing but static artwork without authorization) holds whatever CORS allows.
- The WebSocket already accepts any origin.

**Options:**
1. **Open, as Jellyfin.** Any origin, preflights on every route including `/jellyscale/v1`, and range headers exposed. Fluster, and any browser-engine client, connects with no setup.
2. **An allow-list.** Default origins cover the WebView schemes (`tauri://localhost`, `http(s)://tauri.localhost`), plus origins the operator configures. Fluster works out of the box, while another web client served from elsewhere needs the operator to add its origin. Cost: a setting, and support questions when a client fails silently.
3. **Open by default, with an operator setting to restrict it to an allow-list.** What 1 gives, plus a control for operators who want it. Cost: one setting and its documentation.
4. **Keep as today.** No browser-engine client can connect, Fluster included.

**Who is affected:** everyone who uses Fluster (every jellyscale deployment ships with it), and any future web client hosted elsewhere. The cost of each option in build time is small, and about the same for 1 to 3 (unverified).


Lead's follow-up: failed sign-ins are not bounded today (the user policy reports LoginAttemptsBeforeLockout -1); JS-145 drafted and amended by the product owner.

# Plan change: what DOMAINS.md is for (owner's request, 2026-11-19)

**The owner's words:** "our domains.md file is getting incredibly long. I'm wondering if there are artifacts that exist within it that should probably be moved out, and we can focus on having the domains.md file really being just a file that defines the domains of our software."

**Today:**
- DOMAINS.md is 141 KB in 183 lines. Its sections are Vocabulary, Boundaries, and Invariants grouped by area (Scaling, Data, Messaging, Storage, Compatibility, Transcoding, Security, Play state and sessions, Transcoding continued, Video copy).
- Single invariants run to thousands of words, mixing the rule, its rationale, measurements, test names and history. You have hit this yourself: Read cuts its lines short.
- Every agent that builds or reviews reads it on every task, so its length costs every run in tokens and in attention, and it drifts from the code (JS-093's description).

**The plan today:** JS-093, at priority 36 (behind the identity, library and manifest work). Its description: "Each invariant becomes a rule of one to three sentences with its tests; rationale and measurements move to per-domain files that only tasks in that domain read. Documents only." Its criteria:
1. every invariant is one to three sentences naming its tests, renumbered once;
2. rationale and measurements live in per-domain docs linked from each rule;
3. no rule is lost, by a check that lists every old invariant's tests against the new file;
4. no invariant longer than 600 characters, with stable identifiers, numbers cited in code still resolving, and the regex-over-prose tests removed or replaced by constant-versus-doc checks.

**The owner's framing goes further:** DOMAINS.md defines the domains (each domain's vocabulary, its boundary, what it owns), and what each domain must guarantee is stated briefly there or lives with that domain.

**Decide:**
1. Does JS-093 take the owner's framing? Amend its description and criteria so DOMAINS.md becomes the definition of the domains: what stays in it, what moves, and where.
2. Its priority. It is documents only, and it would shorten every later task's reading. Keep in mind that the identity and library tasks are what viewers feel.
3. Anything that must hold so no guarantee is lost in the move. The DOMAINS invariants are what the checks and reviewers hold builds to, and decisions D-002, D-003 and D-016 cite DOMAINS entries.

# Brief: JS-145, how failed sign-ins are bounded, and what a viewer sees

JS-145 (planned after D-016) bounds failed sign-ins. Before its checks are written, four choices need you. The observations are in (lead's scratch) (real Jellyfin 12.4 in a container, and real jellyfin-web with each answer substituted).

## Observed

**Jellyfin 12.4.**
- By default there is no bound: 14 wrong passwords in a row, each answered 401 in about 77 ms, then the right password works.
- An operator can set `LoginAttemptsBeforeLockout` per user. At that count the account is disabled outright. From then on both a wrong and a right password answer 403, and the account stays locked (still locked after 4 minutes, with nothing suggesting expiry) until an administrator re-enables it.
- An unknown name answers the same 401 as a wrong password.
- Nothing differs by source address (one address tested).

**What jellyfin-web shows for each answer to sign-in:**
| Answer | Viewer sees |
|---|---|
| 401 | "Invalid username or password. Please try again." |
| 403 | "You are not authorized to access the server at this time. Please contact your server administrator for more information." |
| 429 or 503, with or without Retry-After | A "Connection Failure" dialog: "We're unable to connect to the selected server right now. Please ensure it is running and try again." |

No answer makes jellyfin-web say "try again later". The criterion "reads as 'try again later', not as a wrong password or a server fault" cannot be met for jellyfin-web as written. Every answer reads as a wrong password, a refusal by the administrator, or an unreachable server. Fluster can be made to read a 429 correctly (JS-075 records it).

## Choices

**1. What a refused sign-in answers** (the account or address is past the bound):
- a. **401, the same as a wrong password.** The viewer reads "Invalid username or password" even when the password is right, and will retry or doubt their password. The guesser learns nothing. This matches Jellyfin's wording today.
- b. **403.** jellyfin-web says "not authorized… contact your server administrator". This is closest in meaning to a temporary refusal, though it reads as permanent. It is what Jellyfin answers for a locked account.
- c. **429 with Retry-After.** This is the correct HTTP answer and Fluster could say "try again in N minutes", but jellyfin-web shows "server unreachable", which misleads a viewer about the server.
- d. **Slow instead of refuse.** Add a growing delay before answering 401 (for example 1 s, 2 s, 4 s, capped). The viewer sees a slow sign-in and the usual wrong-password text. Guessing becomes slow without anyone being shut out. Delaying holds a request open on the server (an api replica can hold many waiting requests cheaply; unverified at scale).

**2. Per-account lockout vs. the rightful owner.** A hard per-account bound lets anyone keep a named viewer out by guessing their name from many addresses: for as long as the bound lasts, or for ever, as Jellyfin's disable is. The criteria want a stated longest time the owner can be kept out. Options:
- a. A per-account bound that expires after N minutes. The owner can be kept out for N minutes at a time, repeatedly.
- b. Per account, slow only, never refuse. The owner is never kept out, only slowed.
- c. Per address only, refusing. The owner is never kept out by others' guesses, but a guesser with many addresses is not bounded per account.

**3. Behind an ingress with no trusted proxies declared.** Every viewer arrives from the ingress's address. The dogfood runs this way (Kubernetes ingress).
- a. Turn off the per-address bound until proxies are declared, and warn the operator at start-up and in docs/running.md.
- b. Keep it on, keyed by the ingress address. One guesser then slows or refuses every viewer.
- c. Detect a private peer sending forwarded headers and refuse to start until the operator declares proxies. This is safe but costs every existing deployment a configuration step.

**4. Unknown names.** The answer must be the same for a name that exists and one that doesn't (D-014). Counting failures for names that don't exist needs a cap on how many such names are remembered (memory or rows), or the bound applies per address only for unknown names. Choose whether unknown names count toward a per-name bound at all.

**Also:** `LoginAttemptsBeforeLockout` is a per-user policy field clients read. Options: it reports what jellyscale does (for example the per-account count, if there is one), or -1 with the difference listed in compat/differences.yaml. Jellyfin's semantics (disable until an admin re-enables) is option 2 with an infinite N. Keeping Jellyfin's behaviour for an operator who sets it is possible but separate.

Setup: `jellyfin/jellyfin:12.4` (container js145-jf, Docker-assigned port, removed afterwards), wizard completed with the same
/Startup calls as test/differential/run/main.go. Users: admin (admin), alice/bob (password, non-admin). curl only; one source
address (the docker bridge gateway, 172.17.0.1 in Jellyfin's log). Files: (lead's scratch), web.out, web-*.png, env.sh).

## 1. Jellyfin 12.4, POST /Users/AuthenticateByName

Every reply (all statuses below) had `Content-Type: text/plain`, `Server: Kestrel`, `Transfer-Encoding: chunked`, no Retry-After,
no WWW-Authenticate, no rate-limit header. Body of every 401 and 403: `Error processing request.` (same text, no JSON).
Success: 200 `application/json; charset=utf-8`, body `{"User":{...},"SessionInfo":..., "AccessToken":...}`.
Time per wrong attempt ~76-80 ms flat (no growing delay observed over 14 attempts).

| Case | Status | Body |
|---|---|---|
| default policy (LoginAttemptsBeforeLockout = -1, IsDisabled false), wrong password x14 in a row, alice | 401 each, all 14 | Error processing request. |
| right password after those 14 | 200 | normal AuthenticationResult |
| GET /Users/{id} after the 14 failures and the success | LoginAttemptsBeforeLockout -1, IsDisabled false (unchanged) | |
| wrong password, user that does not exist (x4 and earlier x1) | 401 each | Error processing request. (identical to wrong password; 1 ms vs 77 ms) |
| LoginAttemptsBeforeLockout set to 3 via POST /Users/{id}/Policy (204); GET shows 3, IsDisabled false | | |
| wrong #1, #2 | 401, IsDisabled false | Error processing request. |
| wrong #3 | 401 (this reply still 401), GET now shows IsDisabled true | Error processing request. |
| wrong #4, #5 | 403 | Error processing request. |
| right password on the locked account | 403 | Error processing request. (not 200) |
| wrong password on the locked account | 403 | Error processing request. |
| unlock by itself | No. Still disabled/403 at ~4 min (alice, last attempt ~09:53:35, rechecked 09:56:23 and bob 09:57:28). Not checked beyond ~4 min: unverified. | |
| admin sets IsDisabled=false (POST Policy, 204) | right password then 200 | |

Further observations:
- Lock is by account (Policy.IsDisabled becomes true, there is no separate lock state or lock-out time); LoginAttemptsBeforeLockout stays 3.
  The server log says "denied because this account is currently disabled" and `The bob account is currently disabled. Please consult with your administrator.` (log only, not in the HTTP body).
- A successful sign-in resets the failure count: after the right password, two wrong passwords left IsDisabled false and the third disabled it (after re-enable by admin).
- The count is kept while the threshold is -1: bob had 1 failure (from the web test, default policy) before the threshold was set to 3, and was disabled by the 2nd and 3rd of 4 later failures (disabled seen after the 2nd of those; the 2nd reply was 401, the 3rd 403). So earlier failures count toward a later threshold. (Inferred from counts, the count itself is not exposed.)
- Source address: only one real address tested. `X-Forwarded-For: 10.0.0.1..4` sent per failure made no difference (they counted against the same account, locked as without it; the log shows IP 172.17.0.1 throughout, so XFF is ignored without known proxies). - Default for non-admin alice/bob: LoginAttemptsBeforeLockout = -1 and no lockout over 14 failures. Admin account default was not tried: unverified.

Note jellyfin-web calls the lower-case path `/Users/authenticatebyname`; the route was matched case-insensitively.

| 401, empty body | toast: `Invalid username or password. Please try again.` | stays on sign-in |
| 401, JSON body | same as above (body ignored) | same |

# Brief: two known gaps JS-139 must list, but no task or decision covers either

JS-139 makes docs/status.md say truly what is built. Its criterion asks that every known gap be listed with the task that closes it, or "no task" and the decision that accepted it. Two gaps have neither today. The build stopped at Check because there is no honest closer to cite.

## Gap A: every re-encode is H.264 SDR at no more than 1080 lines
**Today:**
- A film that must be re-encoded comes out at 1920x1080 at most, SDR, H.264. That happens when the client can't take the file's video, or picks a quality cap, or an image subtitle is burned in.
- A copy is not capped: a client that plays the file's HEVC or AV1 gets a copy at full size, 4K included. Direct play is full size too.
- The HDR copy's fallback (JS-134) keeps the range but also drops to 1080 lines: "HDR fallback gap: lines above 1080 are lost" (docs/transcoding.md).

**Who sees it:** a viewer on a 4K screen whose client can't play the file's codec, or who turns on a burned-in image subtitle (PGS or VobSub on jellyfin-web) on a 4K film. They see 1080p SDR instead of 4K. How often that happens on the dogfood is unverified.

**Cost of closing it:** a 4K x264 or x265 software re-encode costs several times a 1080p one. The measured x265 fallback figures: 3.2 cores from a 1080p source, 4.0 from 4K (synthetic source, BL-? "measured on testsrc2 only"). JS-135 and JS-136 will measure x264 presets at 4K. What Jellyfin 12.4 does (re-encode at source height and HEVC where the client takes it) is unverified here.

**Options:**
1. **No task.** Accept 1080p SDR H.264 as the re-encode ceiling, with a decision that states why (cost per viewer, client reach).
2. **A task after JS-135 and JS-136** (which give the 4K cost figures): re-encodes keep the source height up to 2160 where the client and the cap allow, possibly in HEVC for clients that take it.
3. **Backlog,** with the question that would promote it.

## Gap B: Dolby Vision profile 5 is always re-encoded
**Today:**
- A profile 5 file has no base layer any other player can show, so it is never copied or direct played to a client that doesn't declare Dolby Vision.
- It is re-encoded and tone mapped to SDR, at 1080 lines (gap A).
- Profiles 7, 8.1, 8.2, 8.4 and 10 copy their base layer, as Jellyfin 12.4 does.

**Who sees it:** a viewer of a profile 5 file, mostly streaming-service web rips. On every client tested (jellyfin-web in Chromium) the cost is a software re-encode with tone mapping. A client that declares Dolby Vision support (Apple TV and some Android TVs, as reported; unverified here) could play it as is. Whether jellyscale would send a profile 5 copy to such a client is unverified.

**Options:**
1. **No task.** Accept that profile 5 is re-encoded for clients without Dolby Vision. No other server can do better, since there is no base layer to copy. State it as a decision.
2. **A task, or a JS-075 criterion:** a client that declares Dolby Vision profile 5 gets a copy, observed on a real device (JS-075 already brings the owner's ExoPlayer and AVPlayer devices).
3. **Backlog** until a client that declares it is in hand.

# Brief: JS-145, the per-address bound in the shipped compose stack, where every viewer arrives from one address

D-020 chose: the per-address bound (10 failures in 15 minutes, then the address refused for 15 minutes) is on only when the operator declares `trustedProxies`. It rejected choice 3b: "keep it on, keyed by the ingress address; one guesser then refuses every viewer". JS-145's criterion also says "the shipped compose stack declares its ingress". The build does what both say. The UX reviewer ran the stack and found that together they produce 3b.

## Measured (UX reviewer, built tree, the shipped deploy/compose stack)
- The stack publishes its Caddy ingress on `127.0.0.1:8096` only. Every client on the host reaches Caddy from the Docker bridge gateway, `172.28.0.1`, and Caddy writes that into X-Forwarded-For, whatever the client sent. The QA reviewer separately observed that Caddy replaces a client-sent header.
- `trustedProxies: ["172.28.0.10"]` (the ingress) is declared, so the api counts `172.28.0.1` for every viewer.
- Ten wrong passwords for ten invented names from the host got 401 each. Then the admin's right password from a new device got **403, Retry-After: 900**, logged as `sign-in refused bound=address address=172.28.0.1 user=admin`. One guesser, or one viewer mistyping 10 times across names, keeps every viewer of the stack out for 15 minutes. jellyfin-web tells them to contact their administrator.
- docs/running.md now says this, and a test pins that text. No decision covers it.

## A related case (QA and architecture reviewers, by reading)
With proxies declared, a request from a declared proxy that carries no usable X-Forwarded-For counts the proxy's own address: no header, every entry itself a declared proxy, or an entry that doesn't parse. All such requests share that one address, which is 3b again for those requests.

## Who is affected
Anyone who runs the shipped compose stack as it ships. How many deployments use it as is, and how clients reach it (on the host, through another proxy on the host, or a published port), is unverified. The dogfood runs on Kubernetes, not this stack, and has no `trustedProxies` today, so its per-address bound is off.

## Options
1. **The compose stack leaves `trustedProxies` out.** The per-address bound is off there, with the start-up warning and metric D-020 asked for. The per-name and known-device bounds still hold. Cost: a household stack has no per-address bound until the operator puts it where clients keep their own addresses and declares it. This changes the criterion "the shipped compose stack declares its ingress".
2. **The stack publishes the ingress on every interface (`8096:8080`) and declares it.** Clients elsewhere on the network may then arrive with their own addresses, but whether Docker keeps a remote client's source address here is unverified. Clients on the host itself would still share the gateway address. Cost: the shipped default becomes reachable from the network, a change of exposure.
3. **The server never applies the per-address bound to an address it cannot attribute to one client.** That means the proxy's own address, a request with no usable forwarded entry, and an address the operator lists as shared (for example the bridge gateway) in a new setting. Such requests rely on the per-name and known-device bounds alone. Cost: more configuration, and a guesser behind that shared address is bounded only per name.
4. **Keep as built.** Accept 3b for the shipped stack, documented as it is now. One guesser can lock every household member out for 15 minutes at a time.

Also needed: for the related case (no usable forwarded entry), choose between counting the proxy's address (as built) and not applying the per-address bound to that request (as option 3 does).

# Brief: JS-145, which address the refusal log names in the shipped compose stack, and triage of what the run left

JS-145 is built to D-020 and D-022 and has passed QA and the adversarial review. One major is open, from the UX reviewer. It is the last thing before the PR.

## The open major: the refusal log names the ingress, not the client

**Today (as built):** each refused sign-in writes one line, `sign-in refused bound=<name|device|address> address=<...> [user=<name>]`. docs/running.md tells operators to alert on `jellyscale_signin_refusals_total` and says "the log line `sign-in refused` says which account and address".

**In the shipped compose stack (D-022: `trustedProxies` absent):** the api does not trust any forwarded header, so `address=` is the api's peer, which is the Caddy ingress container, for every client. The client's address that Caddy forwards in X-Forwarded-For does not appear anywhere in the line. The stack's Caddyfile has no access log, so the client's address is recorded nowhere (read from deploy/compose/Caddyfile, not run).

**Measured (UX reviewer):** with no `trustedProxies`, 20 wrong passwords for one name with `X-Forwarded-For: 203.0.113.9`, then a 21st. The 21st got 403 with Retry-After 900, and the log said `bound=name address=127.0.0.1`. The test peer stood in for the Caddy container. The client's 203.0.113.9 was absent.

**Who is affected:** an operator of the shipped stack investigating a guessing alert. Every refusal names the same address. They cannot tell a guesser from a viewer who mistyped, and they may block the ingress address, which would refuse every viewer. Behind any other ingress where the operator also left `trustedProxies` out, the same holds. The dogfood runs that way today (Kubernetes, no `trustedProxies`). How often operators investigate refusals is unverified.

**History:** before D-022, JS-145's criterion 4 said a refusal through the shipped stack is logged with the client's address as the ingress forwarded it, never the ingress container's own. D-022 changed the declaration and removed that sentence, but recorded no decision about the log.

**Options:**
1. **The log also carries the forwarded header as received, labelled as unverified** (for example `forwarded="203.0.113.9"`), whenever the peer is not a declared proxy. It is never counted toward any bound. docs/running.md says it is what the peer claimed, not checked: true behind the shipped Caddy, which replaces what a client sent (observed), but forgeable when nothing in front rewrites it. Cost: a value a client controls appears in an operator log (quoted, length-capped). An operator who trusts it without reading the docs could be misled.
2. **Caddy in the shipped stack writes an access log** with the client's address and time, and docs/running.md says to match a refusal's time to it. The api log keeps the peer. Cost: a second log to correlate by time, which is imprecise when several viewers sign in at once. The access log also holds every request's path, including item ids (it is the operator's own machine).
3. **Keep as built, and correct the docs.** docs/running.md says that with `trustedProxies` absent the line names the peer (the ingress, in the shipped stack), so it identifies the account, not the client. Cost: an operator of the shipped stack cannot find who is guessing from jellyscale's records at all.
4. **Restore the old criterion: declare the ingress in the shipped stack.** That contradicts D-022 (every client would share one counted address), so it is listed only for completeness.

A related case, already decided by D-022: with proxies declared, a request with no usable forwarded entry is not counted per address, and its log names the proxy's own address (the UX reviewer's minor 13 below). Whichever option you choose could apply to that line as well.

## Minors the run left (for triage: this task, backlog, or drop)

Each was raised by a reviewer and not fixed. The evidence kind is in brackets.

1. **[qa, reading]** A cross-origin page reading Retry-After is checked only as the header string `Access-Control-Expose-Headers: retry-after`, never by a real page on another origin.
2. **[qa, command]** The capture of Jellyfin 12.4 "no bound by default" holds 14 wrong passwords then a right one, a sample rather than an unbounded run.
3. **[adversarial, command]** Under heavy concurrency the unknown-name memory forgets more names than its bound needs. With the bound lowered to 200, 24 parallel workers flooding 4,800 names left 153 remembered, not about 200. The bound holds; no errors. Forgetting early could, at the margin, let a guesser tell a real name from an invented one.
4. **[adversarial, reading]** A right password whose sign-in fails after the password matched, because the client hung up or the database failed at that moment, answers 500 and leaves one counted failure for that name. A viewer on a flaky connection spends counts toward the 20/10 bounds.
5. **[adversarial, reading]** With proxies declared, an ingress that writes the forwarded entry with a port or brackets (`1.2.3.4:5678`, `[2001:db8::1]:443`) turns the per-address bound off for those requests. The only trace is the once-per-process WARN and the unattributed metric.
6. **[ux, reading]** This duplicates the open major: the refusal log names the ingress for every viewer in the shipped stack.
7. **[ux, reading]** compose.yaml says declare the ingress "only when … the ingress has a fixed address (docs/running.md)", but docs/running.md never says how to give it one. A declared container address changes on recreate, and the per-address bound then silently counts the shared address.
8. **[ux, reading]** A viewer refused on a new device sees jellyfin-web's "not authorized… contact your server administrator" with no wait time, though the refusal ends within 15 minutes. This is what D-020 accepted. The reviewer flags it as viewer-visible.
9. **[qa, command]** The transcode e2e gate failed once in a full run (a 500-segment scenario timed out; Postgres was refusing connections near the end of the gate). Both scenarios then passed 5 of 5 alone. The cause is not established, and main was not checked. Sign-in changes are not in that path (unverified).
10. **[qa, command]** The task's own e2e command, with `E2E_ONLY` naming the refused sign-in scenario, fails the cors gate's "checked no JSON responses" summary check, because the filter skips the steps that produce JSON. Run unfiltered, the gate passes 7 of 7.
11. **[ux, reading]** This duplicates 7: the compose comment sends operators to docs that never explain a fixed address.
12. **[ux, reading]** A server run with no ingress logs a WARN naming `trustedProxies` at every start. docs/running.md gives no advice for that case (leave it out, or `[]` so the peer counts). It never mentions that household NAT also makes many viewers share one address.
13. **[ux, reading]** With proxies declared and no usable forwarded entry, the refusal log names the proxy's own address (see "A related case" above).

Decide the major (an option, or evidence first), and for each minor: into JS-145 now, the backlog (with the question that would promote it), or drop.
decisions.tradeoff: In the shipped compose stack (trustedProxies absent, D-022) the refusal log named the api's peer, the ingress container, for every client, and the client's address appeared nowhere; docs/running.md said the line names which account and address.

# Brief: JS-147, what the details page's Audio menu lists when a picked track cannot be delivered

JS-147 makes the details page's Audio menu in jellyfin-web list every audio track the viewer has not hidden, as Jellyfin 12.4 does (captured in compat/captures/audio-menu-12.4). Before JS-147 the item listed only the track the viewer would hear, so the menu offered nothing to pick.

Picking a track other than the one the file plays by default needs the server to make a copy or re-encode with that track (a transcode). jellyscale cannot always do that.

## The states (from the build and its reviews; the first three tested, the last two read)

| State | How long | What JS-147 builds today |
|---|---|---|
| No `transcodeStore` set (a server that only direct plays) | for as long as configured | The menu lists the viewer's track alone, as before JS-147 |
| The film has no probed duration | until it is probed | The menu lists the viewer's track alone |
| No worker is alive, or the only live worker has no cores, or the roles disagree on the store | until the operator fixes it | The menu lists the viewer's track alone. Note: PlaybackInfo itself lists all four tracks here and plays track 1 whatever is picked (reviewer's finding). |
| Every worker is busy right now (no free cores) | seconds to minutes | The menu lists every track; a pick then waits like any transcode (unverified what the viewer sees if it waits long) |
| The transcode for that pick just failed | until retried | The menu lists every track; the pick fails as a transcode fails today (unverified what the viewer sees) |

**Who:** any viewer of a film with several audio tracks on a server in one of these states. The first state applies to a whole deployment that never transcodes. The others are rare on a healthy server; how often is unverified.

## Options
1. **As built.** In the lasting states the menu shows the one track the viewer will hear, so a pick never silently plays something else. In passing states it lists every track, and a pick behaves like any transcode under load. Cost: on a server with no transcoding the menu has nothing to pick, though the file has the tracks (Jellyfin 12.4 would list them and fail or play the default; unverified).
2. **Always list every track.** Show the menu as Jellyfin does in every state. Where the pick cannot be delivered, playback uses the default track or fails with a reason. Cost: a viewer picks a language and hears another, or gets an error, with no hint before playing.
3. **List every track, and refuse a pick with a stated reason where it cannot be delivered** (PlaybackInfo answers an error naming why). Cost: unverified what jellyfin-web shows for that error. It may read as a server fault.
4. **Evidence first:** observe what Jellyfin 12.4 shows and plays when a non-default track is picked with transcoding disabled, before deciding.

Also needed: whether the passing states (busy, just failed) need anything beyond what any transcode does today.
decisions.tradeoff: The details page's Audio menu cannot deliver a pick of a non-default track without a transcode (a browser's direct play plays only the file's default). Where that is impossible for as long as the state lasts (no transcode store, no probed duration, no live worker that runs transcodes, the roles' stores differ) the menu lists the viewer's track alone. Given up, by browser viewers on a deployment with no transcodeStore: they cannot change audio language and hear the file's default; the alternative is every deployment running a transcode store and worker.
decisions.entry: JS-147 lists the viewer's track alone in the lasting states (option 1), and gains three criteria: PlaybackInfo lists no audio track it would not play in those states (the reviewer's finding that it listed four and played the first); an explicit pick made while workers are busy or just after a failure plays or ends in the 'cannot be played at this time' dialog, never another track, while a saved language still falls back to the file's default; docs/transcoding.md tells operators what a server without transcodeStore offers. Always listing every track and refusing at play were rejected: a viewer would pick a language and hear another or hit an error with no hint. What Jellyfin does with transcoding off was not needed to decide. Backlog: the one-track item for clients that switch tracks themselves (unverified), and remembering a viewer's pick per film as Jellyfin 12.4 does.
decisions.serves: PRODUCT.md: each plays on the device in their hand, with the audio and subtitles they chose; Playback never surprises a viewer. DOMAINS 32: the menu offers no track that can't be delivered.

# Brief: JS-147, which audio track the details item names for a client that switches tracks itself, in the states where no transcode can run

D-029 decided: where a pick cannot be delivered for as long as the state lasts (no transcode store, no probed duration, no live worker that runs transcodes, the roles' stores differ), the item lists the track the viewer will hear alone. For a viewer whose saved language (say German, track 2) cannot be delivered there, a browser hears the file's default (track 1), so the item names and lists track 1 (the lead's correction under D-029).

## What changed for another kind of client
Some clients switch audio tracks themselves inside the file (mpv-based players; their profile declares no limit on secondary audio). For them PlaybackInfo, unchanged by JS-147, still direct plays and names the saved-language track 2 in those states, and lists it (a check now guards that, passing). They can play German.

The details item is one answer for every client: it sees no device profile. So after JS-147, in those states, the item names track 1 for the German viewer whatever the client, where before JS-147 it named track 2.

**Who:** a viewer whose saved audio language is not the file's default, on a client that switches tracks itself, on a server in one of the lasting states (a server with no transcodeStore is the common one). Whether any supported native client takes the item's named track as the one to play, rather than PlaybackInfo's, is unverified. Which supported apps switch tracks themselves is unverified beyond docs/transcoding.md naming such clients in general.

## Options
1. **Accept as built.** The item names the track a browser will hear (track 1); a self-switching client's own PlaybackInfo still plays German. Cost: if such a client shows or starts from the item's named track, its viewer sees or hears the default where they could have had German.
2. **The item names the saved-language track (2) and lists it alone.** Cost: every browser viewer's menu shows German over English sound in those states, which D-029 rejected.
3. **The item names 2 but lists 1 alone.** Not possible: a named track is always a listed track (criterion 8).
4. **Evidence first:** observe which supported apps take the item's named audio track when starting playback (JS-075 plays Jellyfin for Android and Swiftfin).

# Brief: JS-152, what a viewer sees when a seek lands on a segment that truly cannot be made

JS-152's criterion 4: "A segment that truly cannot be made is not asked for and refused 500 without end: the viewer gets the app's dialog and the log names the item id, the source id and the reason once per job."

## Observed
- compat/captures/segment-errors-12.4.json (JS-088), jellyfin-web 12.4 against Jellyfin 12.4: when a segment fails after playback has begun, answered 500 or 404, once or every time, jellyfin-web asks for it once, shows no dialog (dialog: false), and the picture stops (pictureGoesOn: false); it does not ask PlaybackInfo again.
- The implementer read jellyfin-web's bundled hls.js error handler: after play() resolves, a segment error calls the load promise's reject, which is then a no-op, so the error event that opens the Playback Error dialog is never raised. Only a media error (bytes the decoder rejects, i.e. a server that lies) takes the other path. Reading only; consistent with the capture.
- A play that starts or resumes at such a segment does get the dialog (a passing check), and the "answered 500 and the player stops asking" check passes: the server side of criterion 4 is met.

## Who
A viewer in jellyfin-web who seeks, mid-play, into a segment the server cannot make. With JS-152's fix the dogfood's case (the audio probe) no longer fails; what remains is a film truly cut short or unreadable at that point. How often: unverified, rare.

## Options
1. Accept for jellyfin-web: the server answers 500 once, stops being asked, and logs the reason once; the viewer sees a stopped picture with no dialog, as with Jellyfin 12.4. The criterion's dialog part applies to a play that starts or resumes there; the seek-after-start scenario records what jellyfin-web shows instead of expecting the dialog. A later task could look for an honest answer that reaches the dialog (none known).
2. Keep the criterion: no build can meet it; JS-152 cannot land.
3. Evidence first: probe jellyfin-web with other honest answers (403, 410, a playlist change) for whether any reaches the dialog.
decisions.tradeoff: JS-152's criterion 4 asked that a viewer get the app's dialog whenever a segment truly cannot be made. jellyfin-web 12.4 raises no dialog for a segment that fails after playback has begun (compat/captures/segment-errors-12.4.json; invariant 37 already says the server can do nothing about it from the failed response). Nothing a viewer has today is lost: before JS-152 the segment was refused 500 without end. Left unmet, for a jellyfin-web viewer who seeks mid-play into a part the file itself cannot give (cut short or unreadable there): the picture stops with no explanation; the operator gets the reason in the log. How often is unverified, thought rare.
decisions.entry: Accepted for jellyfin-web (option 1). Criterion 4 is amended: the 500 is answered once and not without end, the log names item, source and reason once per job, a play that starts or resumes there gets the dialog, and a seek there after playback has begun is pinned by a scenario that asserts one 500, no further request for the segment, no PlaybackInfo and no new job in 30 seconds, and a stopped picture with no dialog, failing if a dialog appears so a change is noticed. Rejected: keeping the criterion (no build can meet it and the dogfood's seek fix would not land); probing 403 and 410 first (invariant 37: the web handler destroys the player on any answer of 400 or more); sending bytes the decoder rejects to force the dialog (a lie on the wire, untested on other clients). 'Jellyfin does it too' is not the reason; no honest answer that reaches the dialog is known. Backlog: a probe for an honest signal (BL-238). Unverified when decided: how often a file-caused failure follows a mid-play seek; the implementer's reading of hls.js's handler (consistent with the capture). Data that reopens it: one dogfood log line of a file-caused segment failure after playback began schedules the probe; a repeat makes it a task ahead of new features.
decisions.serves: PRODUCT.md: Seeking and resuming just work; Playback never surprises a viewer; every failure is reported with its reason, never silent (met for the operator and for a start or resume, unmet for the viewer in the case named). DOMAINS 37.

The refused line's missing method is BL-239: refusals on the dogfood are unverified and no open criterion needs the split; it is promoted by a refusal count above zero on the dogfood for a reason that does not name the method, or by JS-154's decision choosing to refuse with a reason. D-040 is JS-152's, in its own pull request.

# Brief: JS-155 as written costs days of machine time; reshape it?

JS-155 (D-039): each of eight flaky sightings reproduced under CI's shape (ffmpeg 6.1, 2 CPUs) with its failure rate recorded before any fix; a verdict and named cause; fixed where it lies; N of N after; unfound causes brought back as briefs.

## What the run showed (build workflow, 2026-11-20)
- The spec writer encoded the criteria as a checker over a records section in docs/testing.md. To rule a sighting out it required 0 of at least 30 runs, plus a CI-share run of its own of at least 30.
- Measured by the implementer: one CI-shaped share run of a transcode test costs about 14.5 minutes. So ruling out one sighting that does not reproduce takes more than 7 hours, and the worst case over the six transcode sightings is about 43 hours. The deadlock and the e2e sighting each need a full stack per sample.
- After about 25 minutes and 0.76M tokens, the run built only a runner hook in test/integration.sh. No sighting has been investigated.
- What is already known without measuring: the TRUNCATE deadlock (two queue runs) has a named cause in its logs. A worker from an earlier test is still recording a segment when the next test truncates the tables, so a test's worker outlives its test.

## Who is affected
Every PR's landing. Each flake costs one merge-queue run (about 1 hour of CI) and delays the dogfood's redeploy. Five to seven sightings were seen in one day. No viewer has been shown to be affected; whether any sighting is a product race is unverified.

## Options
1. **Reshape JS-155 as a time-boxed investigation, done outside the checks-first workflow.**
   - For each sighting: read its CI log and the code it exercises, then try to reproduce it under CI's shape with a bounded number of runs (for example 20 of the test alone, or 2 hours per sighting at most).
   - Name the cause where found. Fix each found cause as its own small change, with a check that fails before the fix (checks-first, in the normal workflow, a task per product cause).
   - Each sighting not reproduced within the box comes back as a brief with what was tried.
   - The docs record is a short table, not a machine-checked form.
   - Cost: some sightings may end as "not reproduced, cause unknown" sooner.
2. **Keep JS-155 as written.** Days of machine time, and it blocks JS-154 (the 4K measurement needs a quiet machine).
3. **Split it:** a task now for the TRUNCATE deadlock (cause known), the rest to the backlog with a promote rule (for example the same test failing the queue twice more).
decisions.tradeoff: JS-155 as written (D-039) asked for each flaky sighting's failure rate under CI's shape before any fix. Encoded as 0 of 30 runs plus a 30-run share, with one CI-shaped share run measured at about 14.5 minutes, ruling out one sighting costs over 7 hours and the six transcode sightings about 43, on the machine JS-154's 4K measurement needs quiet. After 25 minutes and 0.76M tokens no sighting had been investigated. No viewer is shown affected; whether any sighting is a product race is unverified. Given up by the reshape, by engineers and the dogfood's redeploy: a sighting may end 'cause unknown' inside the box and go on costing about an hour of CI per flake until it fails again.
decisions.entry: JS-155 is reshaped into a task that reads, measures within a box and briefs: every sighting gets, from its queue log, what a viewer would have seen in production (BL-197's heartbeat question among them); reproduction is bounded at 2 hours per sighting and 10 in all under CI's shape, with at least one attempt under the queue's load; verdicts are product, test or cause unknown, and not reproducing is never a verdict of test; no fix lands in it, each named cause comes back as a brief and becomes its own task with a check that forces the condition; no retry, skip or raised timeout; an unknown is promoted when the same test fails the queue again. The table in docs/testing.md is not machine-checked. The TRUNCATE deadlock, whose cause is in its logs (a test's worker outlives its test), is JS-158 at 16, covering or re-stating BL-178. Order, amending D-039: JS-154 to 15, JS-158 at 16, JS-155 to 17; JS-155's log reading may start beside JS-154, its reproduction runs wait for the machine. Rejected: keeping JS-155 as written (days of machine time ahead of a film that did not play); sending the undiagnosed sightings to the backlog unread (the product-race question D-039 raised would be shelved). Data that reopens it: a sighting whose log shows a viewer-visible race, which goes ahead of other open work; or the same unknown test failing the queue again.

# Brief: a 4K HDR film with a burned-in subtitle does not play on the dogfood (JS-154)

Figures and commands: `~/.cache/jellyscale/po/js154-measurements.md`. "Unverified" marks every claim nothing measured.

**What viewers have today.** On the dogfood, a 4K HDR or Dolby Vision film that has to be re-encoded (an SDR screen or a browser that cannot play it as it is, or a PGS subtitle to draw into the picture) is made at 0.56 to 0.63 times real time. The film starts, then stalls and keeps stalling. No message says why. Three plays did this on 2026-11-20 (jobs 82, 83, 85).

**Why.** Three causes, each measured:

1. **The dogfood's processor cannot do this job in real time, with or without the subtitle.** On its own CPU (a 4-core i5-6500, measured in a pod on that node), decoding the 4K picture uses 2.1 cores, tone mapping it to SDR 1.0, encoding 0.4 to 0.6, and drawing the subtitle 0 to 0.1. In all, 3.8 to 4.1 cores for each second of film. The node gives the server 4 cores and its other pods use about 1 of them. Decoding and tone mapping alone already run at 0.83 to 1.0 times real time. **The burn-in is not the cause.** The same film without a subtitle measured the same (0.84 to 0.86x), so every 4K HDR re-encode on the dogfood stalls.
2. **The price is wrong for this machine.** The server prices this job at 3.2 cores. That figure was measured on a much faster 16-thread machine, where the same job does use 2.3 to 2.4 cores. A "core" in the price is a core of that machine. The dogfood's cores do about 1.6 times less work each.
3. **Sharing across the cluster cannot happen with one worker.** Helpers (other workers making chunks of the film ahead of the viewer) start only on another worker, and only when one has room for the job's full price plus room left for a new viewer. The dogfood runs a single worker, so no helper can ever start. The code works as written here. The cluster has 22 processors (nodes of 12, 6 and 4) and the server uses the smallest node's 4.

**Is BL-100 this one?** Probably not. BL-100 is a stall in a test scenario on the test stack's small fixture films ("timed out waiting for playback past 22"), traced to a job-waiting path (Jobs.segment and catchUpSegments). The dogfood failure is the processor's speed. Their mechanisms are unrelated from what the docs say. It is unverified whether that test scenario ever ran slower than real time.

**The measuring pod ran faster than the dogfood did.** On the same CPU, a measuring pod ran today's job at 0.81 to 0.87x where the dogfood's own jobs ran at 0.56 to 0.63x, so real conditions were about 0.7 of the pod's. Why is unverified: other films, the server's own work in the same 4 cores, or a subtitle extraction running alongside. The lead can read the job rows to settle it. **Every figure below that was measured in the pod may be about 0.7 times as fast in the dogfood's own pod.**

**Who is affected, how often.** Every viewer whose client cannot take a 4K HDR or Dolby Vision film as it is, and every viewer who picks a PGS subtitle that the client does not draw itself. jellyfin-web leaves PGS drawing off by default, so in practice every jellyfin-web viewer who turns such a subtitle on. Every such play on the dogfood fails. How many plays that is: unverified. JS-153's decision counters will count them.

## Options

Each option is priced in what the viewer gets, what the owner changes, and what it costs to build. Several can be combined.

**A. The film plays in real time on the dogfood by sharing it across the cluster (helpers).**
- *Viewer:* the film plays at 1080p, tone mapped, subtitle drawn, as promised, if the helpers together reach real time. The first seconds still come from the viewer's own job at about 0.85x (0.6x on the dogfood).
- *How many helpers the server allows:* a helper goes only where it leaves room for another job of the same price somewhere. With two more 4-core workers like the dogfood's, **one** helper runs, about 1.7x in total from pod figures (about 1.2x scaled to the dogfood's 0.6x; unverified end to end). A 12-processor worker allows two helpers on it. Their speed is unverified, because that node's CPU was not measured. A 6-processor worker alone allows none.
- *Needs:* more workers. The dogfood would run a worker role on a second node, k3s-master (12 processors, nearly idle, about 0.4 cores used) or k3s-worker2 (6 processors). That is an owner homelab change: another Deployment or pod with the worker role, the library mounted, the same Postgres and transcode store. The dogfood's transcode store is `file:///data` on a ReadWriteOnce volume, so a second worker would need a shared store (S3 or similar). That is a bigger change, and unverified as the only path. A higher price (option D) raises the room every helper needs with it.
- *Build:* likely none in jellyscale for the sharing itself. The job's price should still match the machine (see D), otherwise the viewer's own worker stays overbooked.
- *Leaves:* a seek still lands on a slow job until helpers catch up (unverified how long).

**B. The iGPU on the dogfood's node (a first hardware slice, BL-040).**
- *What the dogfood's iGPU can do (measured):* the HD 530 (Skylake) **cannot decode 10-bit HEVC**, so the CPU still decodes every 4K HDR film (2.1 cores). Its video processor cannot tone map either. It can tone map through OpenCL and encode H.264.
- *Viewer, measured in a pod on that node:* CPU decode, iGPU tone map (OpenCL) and iGPU encode ran at 1.09x. CPU decode, Jellyfin's faster CPU tone map and iGPU encode ran at 1.10 to 1.12x. That is barely over real time, below the 1.2x the server asks for margin. Scaled by the pod-to-dogfood gap (about 0.7), it is about 0.77x, so it is **not shown to reach real time in the dogfood's own pod**. A seek or a second viewer would stall it, and the node's other pods take the margin. The iGPU encode needed far more bitrate for the same picture at the settings tried, 31 times on a dark scene. A quality-targeted mode was not tried, so the bitrate it would need is unverified.
- *Needs:* the owner gives the pod the GPU (`gpu.intel.com/i915: 1`, the cluster's device plugin, as Jellyfin already has; no privileged container). The image needs the Intel VA driver, plus OpenCL or jellyfin-ffmpeg for the tone map; Alpine's ffmpeg has neither the OpenCL runtime nor `tonemapx` today (unverified for the Alpine packages). The build is a new encode path with its own checks (detection, fallback to CPU, a price per machine).
- *Better hardware in the same cluster:* the other two nodes have newer iGPUs (UHD 630, Coffee Lake and Comet Lake). Those are generally documented to decode 10-bit HEVC and tone map in hardware, which would take most of the CPU load away (**unverified; not measured**). A first slice on those nodes means the worker runs there, which is option A's homelab change too.

**C. A cheaper output when the job is this heavy.**
- *x264 ultrafast in place of veryfast:* 0.91x on the dogfood's CPU. **Does not reach real time.** Same picture at 3.2 times the bytes. Not an option on its own.
- *720 lines in place of 1080:* 1.04 to 1.11x in the pod on the dogfood's CPU, with no margin. With Jellyfin's faster tone map it reached 1.22x, but that needs jellyfin-ffmpeg in the image. Scaled by the pod-to-dogfood gap: about 0.75x and 0.85x, so **neither is shown to reach real time in the dogfood's own pod**. *The viewer loses* 56% of the pixels: softer detail and softer subtitle edges on a large screen. On the dark test scene the measured loss was small (SSIM 0.9911 against 0.9919), and on a detailed scene it would be larger (unverified). D-038 already says an output below 1080 lines is a loss needing this brief. This option breaks the 1080-line ceiling's promise of 1080 for these films.
- *Build:* a rule for when to drop to 720 (by machine speed, not by film), and its checks.

**D. Price the job by what it costs on the worker, so a play the worker cannot hold is refused within seconds with a reason.**
- *Viewer:* instead of a film that starts and stalls, a "cannot be played at this time" message within seconds, and the log names the reason (`cores are short`, with the cost). Nothing plays.
- *What it does on the dogfood:* the measured cost on its CPU is 3.8 to 4.1 cores. A play is refused only when the price is **above the worker's declared cores**. The dogfood declares none and gets 4. A price of 3.9 still fits and still stalls. Above 4.0 it is refused, provided the floor that lets a default worker take the dearest job alone (3.2 today) is not raised with the price, or the dogfood declares fewer cores than the price. Then **every 4K HDR re-encode is refused**, burn-in or not, on every client that cannot take the film as it is. The dogfood worker then holds no such job at all. Today it holds one, which stalls, beside one 1080p SDR re-encode.
- *Elsewhere:* the price is one number for every machine. Raised to 4.1 everywhere, a 16-core worker holds 3 such films instead of 5, although on a fast machine the job uses 2.4 cores. A price per worker, measured or declared by its speed, avoids that. It is a bigger build (unverified size).
- D-038 already ruled this a floor, not the closer. It also fixes the silent stall, and it pairs with A, B or C.

**E. Keep today's behaviour.** The film starts and stalls on the dogfood. A viewer gets no reason. Listed for completeness. It breaks "playback never surprises a viewer" and "every failure is reported with its reason".

## Facts the decision may turn on

- The cause is CPU speed for 4K HDR on one 4-core i5-6500, not the subtitle. Whatever is chosen applies to every 4K HDR re-encode on the dogfood, not only burn-ins.
- In the measuring pod on the dogfood's node, only 720 lines with jellyfin-ffmpeg's tone map cleared 1.2x (1.22x), and the iGPU options cleared 1.0x but not 1.2x. Scaled by the pod-to-dogfood gap, none of them is shown to reach real time in the dogfood's own pod.
- Measured: the dogfood's 4-core node, alone or with its iGPU. Not measured: the 12- and 6-processor nodes' CPUs and their newer iGPUs, and helpers end to end. Options A and B on those nodes rest on unmeasured figures, and they change the owner's homelab: another worker, a shared transcode store, the GPU in the pod.
- Any homelab change (another worker, the GPU in the pod) goes to the owner before it is made.

## Added by the lead
- Why the dogfood ran at 0.56-0.63x where the measurement pod ran at 0.81-0.87x: the dogfood's own log (2026-11-20 22:14:54) shows "image track extraction started" for the same film at the same moment as job 82 (the PGS track read from a 46.7 GB file, BL-234), on the same 4 cores. So on the dogfood a burn-in costs the re-encode plus a concurrent whole-file read; without a subtitle the stall would be the pod's 0.85x.
- Unmeasured: k3s-master (Comet Lake, 12 CPUs, nearly idle; UHD 630, which as a generation decodes HEVC Main10 in hardware and has VPP tone mapping) and k3s-worker2 (Coffee Lake, 6 CPUs, UHD 630). Running the dogfood's worker there, or a second worker there, is a homelab change the owner decides; measuring there first is the same kind of temporary pod the owner approved for k3s-worker1.

# Owner direction (2026-11-21): scale workers up when encoding falls behind

Asked whether the dogfood should refuse 4K HDR re-encodes now (transcodeCores 3), the owner answered instead: "what I'd like to have happen is that we dynamically scale up the amount of pods or something like that as soon as encoding falls behind. I don't know how we do that, if that's done on the operator level, or Kubernetes does that, or we have to do that at the software level." The owner did not approve transcodeCores 3; 4K HDR re-encodes keep stalling on the dogfood until a fix lands.

The lead's reading (product terms; unverified where marked):
- Kubernetes scales: a HorizontalPodAutoscaler (or KEDA) adds and removes worker pods from a metric jellyscale serves on /metrics. jellyscale does not start pods itself (that would tie it to Kubernetes; PRODUCT.md: growing is adding machines; operating stays boring).
- jellyscale's part: (1) a metric that says "encoding is falling behind" (for example: re-encodes running under real time with no helper available, or plays refused for lack of capacity, from JS-153's decision counters and the transcode state); (2) workers that join mid-film and share a slow job already exist (helpers, failover); (3) a worker must be runnable as its own Deployment (the dogfood runs every role in one pod); (4) workers must share the transcode store (the dogfood's is a ReadWriteOnce local volume; S3 or RWX).
- The operator's part: the example manifests (JS-056) could ship the worker Deployment with an autoscaler example; the dogfood would need the shared store (the owner: decide after JS-162/JS-163's figures).
- Limit: a new pod takes seconds to tens of seconds to start (unverified); the viewer who triggers the scale-up may still wait or be refused briefly; a minimum of two workers hides that. Scaling down must not cut a job mid-film (graceful worker stop exists: unverified for this use).
- On the dogfood, extra pods only help on nodes with idle CPUs (k3s-master: 12 nearly idle; JS-163 measures).

The owner did not approve the interim refusal by configuration. Given up, by the dogfood's viewers: every 4K HDR re-encode keeps stalling with no reason until workers run on other nodes (JS-166), which waits on JS-162's and JS-163's figures and the owner's store decision. Given up, by operators: the autoscaler needs something beside Postgres (a metrics adapter or KEDA), so it stays optional. Given up, by viewers on any cluster at its maximum or while a worker starts: a refusal with a reason (JS-161), not a wait. Unverified when decided: that more workers bring the film to real time end to end; how long a worker pod takes to start; that a worker removed without a replacement costs no stall.

decisions.brief: brief-js162.md with js162-measurements.md: helpers end to end in jellyfin-web on 2-CPU workers (one run per configuration, 5 minutes after the seek, a shared local directory). As built, two equal workers play a 4K HDR re-encode exactly as one does (no helper ever starts; 302 to 304 refusals per play for the room kept for a new viewer, with one viewer and nothing queued); three hold real time until a seek, then 0.72 to 0.84x because the helper left behind runs on unbounded (5 min 25 s, to the film's end in another run); a 2-CPU and a 6-CPU worker play it only if the job lands on the large one (it landed on the small one in 2 of 2 first plays). With the room rule lifted: three workers real time throughout, two until the seek, small plus large throughout. Options A (keep), B (bound a helper by its viewers), C (drop the room rule), D (place the job on the worker that holds it), B with C.
decisions.tradeoff: Whether room held empty for a viewer who has not asked is worth a film stalling beside an idle worker; and, once helpers may fill every worker, who gives way when a second viewer arrives: the viewer already watching (their helpers stopped, a stall) or the newcomer (a refusal with its reason).
decisions.entry: A is rejected. B is JS-167 at 15 (a helper no viewer's place bounds stops within 5 seconds). C is JS-168 at 16 (no room is held back for a viewer who has not asked; two equal workers must hold the film before and after a seek, three runs, which also proves B with C; a second viewer's arrival is observed there). D is JS-161's placement criterion made exact (10 of 10 plays on the worker that holds the job). JS-161 moves to 17, depends on both and gains two rules, because as written it would refuse every play JS-162 saw helpers carry (those workers were counted 3.2 cores by the floor it removes): a play no one worker holds but the workers with room hold together is admitted; and a viewer watching at real time is never taken under it by a newcomer, so, as a default that JS-168's second-viewer figures confirm or change by a brief before JS-161's Spec, a helper of a job its own worker does not hold at 1.2 times real time alone is held as that play's own and the newcomer is refused with its reason and counted as demand. decisions.brief: brief-js163.md with js163-measurements.md, and the owner's direction of 2026-11-21 (detect the hardware and choose the best configuration automatically; fine-tuning allowed, never needed). On both UHD 630 nodes, in Jellyfin's image with jellyfin-ffmpeg, a 4K HDR re-encode done wholly on the GPU ran at 3.9 to 5.2 times real time for 0.16 to 0.28 CPU-seconds per second of film (4.1 to 7.2 on the processors), three at once at 1.5 to 2.0x each (video-processor tone map rows), at 0.97 to 1.47 times x264's bytes for equal SSIM on two fairly dark scenes; with an OpenCL tone map, one job at 3.85 to 3.97x for 0.5 to 0.7. No GPU tone map gives today's picture: the video processors' are about two thirds darker (VAAPI) and a third brighter (QSV) with no parameters; OpenCL with the hable curve is about a quarter darker, the same as jellyfin-ffmpeg's processor tone map. Today's colour tag options fail after GPU decode in ffmpeg 8; the same tags in the bitstream work.
decisions.tradeoff: Whether hardware encoding enters ahead of its place in the road, and what picture a viewer may be given for the speed: every measured GPU path changes an HDR film's brightness from the processor's.
decisions.entry: BL-040 is promoted on D-044's own reopen clause (a UHD 630 holds the job at 1.2x within twice x264's bytes), not on the request. JS-169 (measure, in jellyscale's own image, whether a GPU tone map with a set curve reaches the processor's picture; bytes on a bright scene and by a second measure; memory and jobs at once; the seam) enters at 20 and may run beside the builds ahead of it. JS-170 (first slice: Intel VAAPI/QSV, detected by a real test of each stage at start, chosen per job, processor otherwise) enters at 27 after JS-041 and JS-157, and moves to directly after JS-166 if JS-166 does not close the stall on processors or the dogfood counts a refusal for cores with every worker running. JS-054 keeps NVIDIA, AMD, hardware decode for processor streams and outputs above 1080 lines. 'Best configuration' is a rule of outcomes: the same picture first, then holding 1.2 times real time as measured on that worker, then no more than twice x264's bytes in a quality-targeted mode, then the least processor; otherwise the processor for that job, with the reason logged and counted (the HD 530 is the negative case). One film has one picture whatever the hardware: the driver video-processor tone maps are never used, by default or by override; a GPU tone map is accepted only within 5% (or one 8-bit code value, whichever is more) of the processor path's brightness above black and at SSIM 0.99 or above on three scenes; if no setting reaches that, the options return as a brief, among them moving the processor path to the shared curve, which would be a changed guarantee and is not taken here. Operators may set per worker hardware off, the device and the most hardware jobs at once, and nothing else; none is needed. Given up, by operators: the speed the video-processor tone maps have over the candidate path (up to a third) and their lower processor cost (0.16 to 0.28 CPU-seconds per second against 0.5 to 0.7, so 2 to 4 times), and with it some of the jobs one GPU node holds at once (three were measured on the rejected path, none yet on the candidate). Nothing by viewers. Unverified when decided: every figure in jellyscale's own image; the byte bound beyond two dark scenes of one film (SSIM margin about 0.0003); memory per job; the GPUs shared with other apps; whether any setting matches the picture; what brightness difference viewers notice (the 5% is the product owner's, to be argued with frames). Data that reopens it: JS-169 showing no path within the bound, or bytes past twice x264's on a bright scene; an operator's measured case where the automatic choice was wrong.

decisions.entry: JS-166 runs a processor worker on the 12-thread node beside the 4-core node's worker, which stays as helper and failover; no worker goes on the 6-processor node until it can use its GPU. The GPUs of both UHD 630 nodes are used when JS-170 lands and not before: nothing is deployed for hardware jellyscale cannot yet use.
