decisions.entry: A helper is never claimed by a worker that is running a viewer's, a seek's or a failover's job of its spec, and with one worker no helper is queued or claimed whatever its free cores; a worker running only helpers of the spec may still take another after the one-second wait when it has the cores. JS-168 criterion 6 is made exact so, the older checks stand unamended but for one subcase (D-053), and docs/transcoding.md and DOMAINS.md invariant 58 state the rule. Rejected: allowing same-worker helpers (C: ten checks amended for a speed-up nobody measured); measuring first (D: holds a merge for an answer that would not change what lands); forbidding every second job of a spec on a worker (A: could take a large worker's second helper, unverified whether the 2+6 runs used one). Given up: the same-worker helper a lone worker with room for three jobs got before JS-168, read from the old code and never measured, by nobody known. Unverified when decided: whether a same-worker helper speeds a slow job on a worker with idle cores; whether any JS-168 long run had a helper beside a viewer's job on one worker (such a row is run again, holding nothing). Data that reopens it: a measurement of a same-worker helper reaching 1.0x on idle cores; the dogfood showing a job under 1.2x on a worker with the job's cost free and no other worker to help.

decisions.brief: brief-d052-capacity.md: one check unchanged since 30af59c (the 'not queued' half of the helper capacity check) wants a helper row queued on a lone 16-core worker holding 3.2 cores, which D-052's lone-worker rule forbids; on a trial of D-052 it fails with 0 rows, want 1; its 4-core case and its 'not claimed' sibling pass. Options: A (give the 16-core subcase a second worker running nothing of the spec and want the row there), B (keep the check, a lone worker helps itself), C (hold the fix for a measurement).
decisions.tradeoff: D-052 said every check that passed on 30af59c passes unamended; one subcase asserts exactly what D-052 gave up, so no build passes both.
decisions.serves: JS-168 criterion 6: 'with one worker nothing changes: no helper is queued or claimed, whatever cores the worker has free'. PRODUCT.md: 'A heavy film uses the whole cluster's processors rather than stalling on one machine while others sit idle.' docs/transcoding.md: 'No helper can start with one worker.'
decisions.entry: The 16-core subcase of the helper capacity check gains a second 16-core worker running nothing of the spec and wants the helper queued for it; the 4-core subcase and the 'not claimed' check are unchanged, and the amended case still fails on a build that queues nothing. It is the one exception to D-052's 'older checks stand unamended', named in JS-168 criterion 6 and cited as D-053 in Changed guarantees; any other old check that contradicts D-052 comes back as its own brief. The three JS-168 waits return to their 30af59c text (two helpers beside the main job) as a consequence of D-052, not an amendment. Rejected: B (reopens the regression D-052 closes; no rule separating a large lone worker from it is designed or measured); C (holds a merge for a measurement, rejected in D-052 and by the owner on 2026-11-21). Given up: the check's assertion that a lone worker with the cores queues a helper for itself, by operators of one large worker with transcodeHelpers on, number unknown, who were already told a lone worker gets no helper; the dogfood's 4-core case is unchanged. Unverified when decided: whether that queued row was ever claimed on a real film or sped one (the check shows a queued row only). Data that reopens it, as D-052: a measurement of a same-worker helper reaching 1.0x on idle cores; the dogfood showing a job under 1.2x on a worker with the job's cost free and no other worker to help.

decisions.brief: brief-d054-version-slots.md and the lead's follow-up of 2026-11-22. First: the subtest 'an idle worker of another version does not count as a slot for a viewer: a helper is preempted for the next viewer' of TestOutputVersionAcrossProcesses (from JS-082 and JS-087, unchanged since) sets up a lone version-4 worker running the first viewer's job and a helper of that job on the same worker, which D-052 forbids; on the D-052 build it gives up after 1 minute waiting for that helper. Options then: A (the helper is one a second version-4 worker's job is helped by; assertions unchanged), B (keep the check, a lone worker of a version helps its own viewer's job), C (drop the helper from the subtest). Follow-up: with the setup amended (two version-4 workers of one and two slots) and the assertions unchanged, the subtest passes on the D-052 build (27 s) and also on a build that counts every version's workers (33 s), one run each on one host, because the rescue added in the D-052 fix round (a viewer's job that has waited half the queue timeout, 3 s of 6 s, stops the helpers it needs, with the same reason) stops the helper and the viewer still gets a segment; the in-package check of the same invariant does fail on the counting build and passes on the D-052 build. Options now: A (add one assertion: the helper was stopped when the third viewer asked, not by the rescue), B (assertions unchanged, drop the condition that the subtest fails on a counting build, the in-package check being the guard), C (hold #247 for another design across processes).
decisions.tradeoff: D-052 and D-053 said the older checks stand unamended but for one subcase; this subtest's setup needs the same-worker helper D-052 gave up, so no build passes both. With the setup amended, its unchanged assertions no longer tell a build that counts the viewer's version only from one that counts every version, because the half-timeout rescue reaches the same end about 3 s later: the proof across processes is kept only by adding an assertion, or given up.
decisions.decision: accept (option A of the first brief for the setup; option A of the follow-up for the added assertion)
decisions.serves: DOMAINS.md invariant 59: 'Capacity accounting (free cores, helper preemption, `Unavailable`) counts the viewer's version only.' JS-082: 'A slow job's helper is made by a worker of the job's version or by none'. JS-087: 'only live workers and jobs of the replica's output version count'. PRODUCT.md: 'Play starts in seconds and keeps up.' and 'Nothing breaks the viewers' evening. Upgrades, a lost machine and a database failover happen without interrupting anyone.' JS-168 criterion 6: 'A helper is never claimed by a worker that is at that moment running a viewer's, a seek's or a failover's job of its spec.'
decisions.entry: The subtest's setup is amended, its assertions are kept and one is added. Setup: two version-4 workers, so the helper holding the slot the third viewer needs runs, by the product's own rule and with no change to the server for the test, on the version-4 worker that is not running the viewer's job; when the third viewer asks, no version-4 worker has the job's cost free without that helper's slot and w5 is idle with room. Assertions kept: the third viewer gets a segment and the helper is cancelled with 'a new viewer needed its slot'. Assertion added: the helper was stopped at the third viewer's ask and not by the half-timeout rescue, read from the rows' own times (the helper ended before the third viewer's job had waited half the queue timeout), with no wall-clock bound of the test's that a slow machine could miss. Conditions: a recorded run of the subtest failing on a build that counts every version's workers, on the added assertion, and a recorded run passing on the build; the in-package check of the same invariant stays unamended and stays shown failing on that build; every other subtest of the test stands unamended; no test-only knob enters the server. If either run does not come out so (the stop and the job's creation being one instant is reasoned, not run), it comes back as a brief with the run's output and option B is not taken by default. It is the second exception to D-052's 'older checks stand unamended', after D-053: JS-168 criterion 6 names it beside the 16-core subcase, and Changed guarantees cites D-054 for the amended setup and the added assertion; any further old check that contradicts D-052 comes back as its own brief (internal/transcode and internal/api were still running when this was first decided). Rejected: of the first brief, B (reopens the regression D-052 closes; no rule separating a lone worker of a version from a lone worker is designed or measured) and C (drops the proof with real processes that a viewer preempts a helper when the only free room is another version's); of the follow-up, B (gives up the proof across processes that version counting is right rather than rescued, when an assertion that keeps it has not been tried: a counting error would delay each start of play by about 3 s during an upgrade and only a one-process check would notice) and C (holds a merge for a design nobody has, while A needs two short runs). Given up: the proof across processes that the lone worker of a version helps its own viewer's job, which D-052 already gave up; in product terms, during an upgrade the last worker of the old version gets no helper for its viewers' job while workers of the new version sit idle, so a job that worker makes below real time stays slow until the roll ends, unmeasured, by viewers on the old version mid-upgrade, number unknown and none known. Nothing viewers have changes by this amendment itself. Noted, not a loss: since the rescue, a version-counting error across processes costs a viewer about 3 s and not a 503 (one run on the counting build), which is why the old assertions alone no longer catch it; the old one-worker setup would be masked the same way (reasoned, not run). Unverified when decided: that the helper's end and the third viewer's job's creation are the same instant on the build, and at least 3 s apart on the counting build; whether in the first failing run a helper row was queued that no version-4 worker could claim, and whether such a row counts against a viewer's room; whether any other old check contradicts D-052; every figure here is one run on one host. Data that reopens it: as D-052 (a measurement of a same-worker helper reaching 1.0x on idle cores; the dogfood showing a job under 1.2x on a worker with the job's cost free and no other worker to help); a capture or dogfood log of a viewer stalled or refused during an upgrade walked in the documented order while the lone worker of its version had the job's cost free, or of a queued helper row that no worker may claim holding room a viewer needed; the added assertion failing on the build in CI for a reason that is the machine's and not the build's; the dogfood's logs showing helpers stopped by the half-timeout rescue while a worker of another version sat idle, which is a counting error the rescue is hiding.

decisions.brief: brief-js173.md and its follow-up: JS-173's fix has Refusal read its live-job check and its count of cores in one read-only snapshot, and has a worker's write that ends a job mark that worker seen (seen_at) in the same statement, whatever its liveness lock, so invariant 25's sentence 'Only a locked worker claims, forgets others and refreshes seen_at; a relocking one only reads its own row' is no longer literally true. Follow-up, by the lead's reading: the write is an UPDATE of the worker's row and never inserts; the liveness reaper does not read seen_at; but every reader other than Refusal counts a worker by seen_at alone within 10 s (alive and deliverability of a picked audio track or burnt-in subtitle, store agreement, the reason after a queue timeout, the room that a worker's placement, helpers and helper preemption see), and did before JS-173. Option B (refresh only with the lock held) built in a scratch copy: both sightings' checks pass 3 of 3, so the stopped-and-continued worker holds its lock, but TestAViewerWhoseJobCostsTwoGivenUpJobsTogetherIsNotRefused fails 3 of 3 on its precondition, undiagnosed, and passes 3 of 3 on the JS-173 build. Options: A2 reword and name the readers; A3 the same plus a follow-up making those readers lock-aware; B; C hold JS-173 until the readers are lock-aware.
decisions.tradeoff: Whether a fix that ends a wrong 'cannot be played' merges now with a stated, unmeasured widening (readers that count a worker by seen_at alone count a relocking worker for up to 10 s after it ends a job, as they already do after it loses its lock), or waits for a change to worker liveness or to those readers.
decisions.decision: accept (option A3: the sentence is reworded with the exception and the readers named; the readers' lock-awareness goes to the backlog)
decisions.serves: PRODUCT.md goal 1: 'Playback never surprises a viewer. Starting, seeking, resuming, and recovering from a failure just work, for every film.' 'Failures are invisible.' 'every failure is reported with its reason, never silent'. DOMAINS.md invariant 25: 'Losing the liveness lock is not yet losing the lease'.
decisions.entry: Invariant 25's sentence is reworded: only a locked worker claims and forgets others, and only a locked worker's look refreshes seen_at; the one exception is the write by which a worker ends one of its own jobs, which marks that worker seen whatever its lock, changes its row only if it is still there, and never restores a forgotten worker's row; PlaybackInfo's refusal for cores still does not count a relocking worker; the readers that count a worker by seen_at alone are named, with what they may now do for up to `counted` after a relocking worker ends a job. JS-173 merges with that text. Given up: a viewer whose request (a picked audio track, a burnt-in subtitle, a job left for that worker, a helper not preempted) falls in that window on a worker that never retakes its lock may wait up to the queue timeout (6 s) or the rescue before being answered; before JS-173 the same held only for the 10 s after a lock loss. The fix changes when a worker is marked seen, not what a lease guarantees. Rejected: B (one of JS-173's checks fails 3 of 3 on it for an undiagnosed reason, and it is a fix round in worker liveness to protect readers that were never lock-aware); C (holds a fix for a wrong refusal forced 3 of 3, for a window no one has seen); A2 alone (the readers' gap would be stated and then forgotten). The first condition of this decision's earlier form held (the write never inserts); the second failed by the lead's reading and is answered here. A new backlog item holds making those readers count a worker only with its lock held. Triage with it: the record gains one line saying the first sighting's literal order passes on the unfixed tree and which stricter order forces it; which give-up paths the forced checks show (criterion 4) is asked of the lead, and any path not shown becomes a task beside JS-161 that does not hold this merge. Unverified when decided: how often a worker relocks for more than 10 s and ends a job meanwhile (none seen); the viewer's wait in the worst case (derived, not measured); why B changes the order in the two-jobs check, and whether that says anything about the build that merges (it passes there 3 of 3). Data that reopens it: the dogfood's logs showing a worker relocking for longer than `counted`; a queue timeout or late start within `counted` of a worker losing its lock; a job admitted for cores to a worker that does not hold its lock; JS-161 or JS-164 making one of the named readers decide an admission or a gauge, which promotes the backlog item into that task's design review.

decisions.task: JS-161, JS-166, JS-045, JS-060 and the viewer-facing set

Options: the order as is; the viewer-facing set after JS-161 and JS-166; the set first; other. (brief-triage-0522.md)

decisions.serves: PRODUCT.md, The road there: 'each stage usable on its own', stages 3 (People) and 4 (A living library) before 5; goal 1 for JS-161 and JS-166.
decisions.entry: Option (b), amended. JS-161 and JS-166 stay first on the dogfood's measured stall (JS-154). The viewer-facing set then goes ahead of all remaining measurement, tuning, GPU and autoscaling work, in the road's order: JS-041, JS-127, JS-033, JS-036, JS-037, JS-045, JS-047, JS-060 at 25 to 32, then JS-157 and JS-150; JS-164, JS-169, JS-170 and the rest follow at 35 to 51 with their content unchanged. decisions.brief: Two checks of a cut source read during a re-encode fail on main: the waiting request got a 24-byte non-segment answer in under 200 ms instead of a segment from a fresh job (2 of 3 on main; 3 of 3 passed on the JS-168 tree), and the persisting-cause case got no failure (queue run 45086436037, and #225's run on 2026-11-20). Viewer effect reasoned, unverified. Options: a task now, before or beside JS-161, or backlog. (brief-triage-0522.md)

decisions.entry: JS-159 moves from 25 to 16 and builds beside JS-161. The persisting-cause sighting is its own. It gains three criteria: both cut-read cases run 20 times on main under CI's shape first, with what the 24 bytes are and whether the waiting-request case shares its cause; if not, that case returns as a brief and is not built here; after the fix both pass 20 of 20 with no check weakened. docs/status.md lists the gap against JS-088 until it merges. Each failure costs about 45 minutes and a requeue. Options: move JS-158 ahead; a task that triages the recurring flakes into causes; both; leave as is. (brief-triage-0522.md)

JS-175 enters at 22: a verdict from the log for each of the 12 failed runs, product causes back as briefs with nothing in the product changed, a forcing check and a fix only for a test cause seen twice, reproduction within 8 hours, the timed-out shard split if its healthy time is within 10 minutes of the timeout (takes BL-175), and the next 10 queue runs counted. (brief-triage-0522.md)

decisions.entry: Both JS-168 minors are already criteria of JS-161 (D-050) and are dropped as covered. The lease-keeper check and the flood tests' time go to JS-175 (criteria 6 and 5). JS-172's replaced check is accepted as built: it fails on a build that exceeds the ceiling, and the lost race-forcing check is BL-251, promoted on any row count over the bound or the next change to the cap. The docs word-presence finding is dropped under BL-020. BL-175 is taken by JS-175.

decisions.brief: A rolling restart of a worker that declares nothing (brief-js161-restart.md): JS-161's worker measures its speed (bound 15 s; 6.1 to 7.6 s on a CI runner) before it registers, so a segment request waiting through a restart passes the 6 s queue timeout and is refused (test/roles.sh, queue run 45132952457). A worker that declares transcodeCores or transcodeSlots now registers at once and measures beside its work. Options: A keep, B count the reference speed until measured, C register at once for work already admitted only, D shorten the measurement, E hold JS-161.
decisions.tradeoff: Given up until JS-176 merges: on a cluster whose workers declare nothing and restart without a surge, with no other worker with room, a request in flight during the restart can be refused and a picture already playing freezes. The dogfood declares 3 and is unaffected.
decisions.entry: JS-161 merges with option A as a dated gap, not a rule: an undeclared worker registers only after measuring (bound 15 s), so on a cluster with no other worker with room a request in flight during a restart can be refused, and a picture already playing freezes. Given up until JS-176 merges, by viewers of clusters whose workers declare nothing and restart without a surge; the dogfood declares 3 and is unaffected. docs/status.md, docs/running.md and Changed guarantees say so, citing this. The guarantee is kept by option C as JS-176 at priority 20, which JS-166 depends on: a replacement registers at once for work already admitted and counts nothing for new plays until measured. Rejected: B (admits on a guess, the silent stall JS-161 removes), D (does not close the window and adds noise to a figure measured at 0.19 and 0.46 on one host), E (the dogfood's measured stall waits). Advising operators to declare capacity is a stopgap and leaves the docs with JS-176. Start-time measurement noise goes to the backlog (BL-252). Reopens on: JS-176's design review showing C needs more than one build (it returns as a brief), or a refused in-flight request on any deployment before it merges (JS-176 moves directly after JS-161). Superseded by D-062 (2026-11-23): the facts it rested on were corrected; its gap never ships.
decisions.serves: PRODUCT.md: 'Nothing breaks the viewers' evening. Upgrades, a lost machine and a database failover happen without interrupting anyone.' D-044: capacity is measured on the worker at start, not declared.

decisions.brief: Minors and observations left by JS-159 and JS-161 (brief-triage-0523.md): a segment re-read on every poll; an unmeasurable segment held with no trace; the exit-first order covered only by natural runs (failed 2 of 32 on main, 20 of 20 after the fix); failures not countable across a restart, so JS-159 criterion 6 could not be taken; a run returned clean with QA items unfinished; nine capacity and admission notes on JS-161; JS-161's recorded jellyfin-web measurements not done.
decisions.tradeoff: Given up: the dogfood count of jobs that failed after storing a segment before the fix (JS-159 criterion 6), so whether a cut-short segment was stored there is not known, and any leaves with transcodeRetention; a forced check of the exit-first order; two of three second-viewer runs of each kind and the developer-machine shared-play runs of JS-161. No viewer or operator loses a capability.
decisions.entry: No new task and no priority moved. JS-175 criterion 7 counts the two cut-read cases apart in its 10 queue runs, one failure returning JS-159 as a brief; no hook in the worker. JS-176 gains criterion 5: /metrics shows as capacity for new plays only what admission counts while a worker is unmeasured. JS-164 criterion 2: a held-film refusal carries its own reason from whichever replica refuses. JS-079 gains criterion 5: a worker of the previous release is not counted as a partner for a shared play unless it says it can help. JS-159 criterion 6 is closed as not taken; docs/running.md says jellyscale keeps no history of ended jobs and that counts across restarts come from scraping /metrics and keeping logs; no failure history is built. JS-161's shared-play measurement is taken by JS-166 criterion 3 on the dogfood, and its second-viewer measurement is one run of each kind beside the next task. docs/transcoding.md marks the i5-6500's 2.7 as computed until the dogfood's measured figure replaces it; the SMT question and the single-benchmark question are answered by that reading and JS-166 criterion 9. Backlog: BL-253 (segment re-read per poll), BL-254 (unmeasurable segment held silently), BL-255 (a clean run with QA items unfinished; build.js changes on a second occurrence), BL-256 (stale shared-placed queued job holds cores), BL-257 (timed-out measurement counted at reference speed; promoted on a dogfood measurement over 7.5 s or a timed-out line), BL-258 (a film held 60 s after its viewer leaves). JS-176 starts now; JS-174 runs beside it, never ahead. Reopens on: a cut-read failure in the counted runs; an early-input-end failure counted on the dogfood after the fix; the dogfood's measured capacities changing which rows a node holds.
decisions.serves: PRODUCT.md: 'every failure is reported with its reason, never silent'; 'Nothing breaks the viewers' evening. Upgrades, a lost machine and a database failover happen without interrupting anyone.' DOMAINS.md invariant 40. Owner, 2026-11-22: nothing outruns the product.

decisions.brief: D-060 reopened with corrections (brief-js161-reopen.md): the roles, e2e and differential stacks declared transcodeCores only because JS-161's build added it; the dogfood declares 3, so holding JS-161 changes nothing there; the suite itself meets the gap (queue run 45135324010, 9 cmd/jellyscale tests). Measured with 4 test processes on 4 pinned CPUs: an undeclared worker's speed 0.174 to 0.732 (capacity 0.70 to 2.93 on 4 processors), a 720p re-encode refused as 'cores are short' until the next start; a worker registering 5.3 s after start and the waiting request refused at 6.0 s; the benchmark beside live jobs timing out or reading 0.105 to 0.109 while those jobs ran at 0.586x and 0.95x. Options: A hold JS-161 for a redesign, B merge without the start-up measurement, C change what is measured then merge, D amend the 9 checks.
decisions.tradeoff: Given up, by operators who declare nothing on a CPU slower per core than the reference machine or on SMT threads, and by their viewers: the refusal with a reason for a play that worker cannot hold; it is admitted and stalls, as on main, with the operator told once in the log and on /metrics. D-044's 'capacity is measured on the worker at start, not declared' is set aside until a measurement exists that a busy host does not move and that slows no film. The dogfood declares its capacity and is unaffected. No viewer loses anything main gives.
decisions.entry: Option B. JS-161 merges without any benchmark, at start or beside work: an undeclared worker counts each processor at the reference speed with no floor, registers at once, and says in its log and on /metrics that its capacity is assumed; transcodeCores is the way to be exact, and docs/running.md says when an undeclared worker overstates itself and how to choose the figure. JS-161 criterion 2 is replaced, 3, 5 and 9 read 'declared' for 'measured', 7 names transcodeCores on an assumed worker, and a new criterion 12 returns the roles, e2e and differential stacks to undeclared workers and requires the 9 failed tests to pass unamended; one that still fails returns as a brief. D-060 is superseded: its gap never ships and its Changed guarantees and docs lines are removed. JS-176 is dropped and JS-166 no longer depends on it; JS-166 criterion 9 records declared capacity against job speeds. Of D-061: JS-176 criterion 5 is void (its substance is JS-161 criterion 2), JS-161's build is next with JS-174 beside it, BL-257 closes, and the i5-6500's 2.7 stays marked computed. BL-252 closes into BL-259 (an undeclared slow or SMT worker counts more than it holds), which carries what a measurement must meet: no delay to registration, no film slowed, a figure a busy host does not move, shown on a 4-process run. Rejected: D (the suite would stop showing measured viewer losses, and two of the checks guard existing guarantees), C (an unpriced redesign with unverified leaves ahead of JS-166), A (holds JS-166 for a capability the merge does not need). Reopens on: the assumed-capacity slow reason counted on any deployment; JS-166 showing a declared figure wrong by more than a fifth; JS-056 starting; any of the 9 tests failing after the measurement is out.

decisions.brief: Left by JS-158 (brief-triage-js158.md): three product statements its record read from code and saw in no run (the dead-node reap against the job end of a worker forgotten while it lives; a pending migration altering two worker tables in a rolling upgrade; a stream replica's snapshot read aborted by that migration); three test-kit minors (five forced checks passing on today's kit, cmd/jellyscale's guard not seeing Postgres sessions and the stress driver's fake workers outside it, fresh() restarting a kept worker); spec writers twice in one day matching mixed-case patterns against the lowercased doc, each stopping a build on a dispute.
decisions.tradeoff: Given up: nothing a viewer or operator has. Left as they are, on no data that anyone meets them: a stall of up to a lease (about 30 s, unverified) for the viewers of a job whose end a deadlock with the reap aborts, and up to 5 s in which a stream replica whose snapshot read a migration aborted cannot answer from memory if Postgres also goes away.
decisions.entry: No new task and no priority moved. JS-079 gains criterion 6: a migration that locks two tables a running worker and a stream replica use, applied under a playing film with real processes, leaves the upgrading replica started or refusing once with a message naming the lock, and no viewer request answered an error; what a replica answers from memory after an aborted snapshot read is recorded and returns as a brief, not built. JS-079 is split into migrations (1, 3, 6) and mixed-version play (2, 4, 5) when it starts. decisions.brief: brief-js177-design.md: four decisions before JS-177's Spec, from its design review. (3) Whether the figure survives a restart: Postgres by hardware class with a 24 h expiry, not at all, or per pod or node; about 40 s to converge on a start that overstates (design, not measured). (4) What learning cannot see: the worker's own extractions beside a transcode, and contention the kernel does not show; state as limits, count extraction CPU, or measure first.

decisions.brief: Quick Connect: a signed-in account can try 6-digit codes against approvals. Options: (A) bound failed approvals per approving account; (B) per account, and per address when trustedProxies is declared; (C) per address only; (D) no bound. Candidate limits: 10 failures in 15 minutes, 15 minutes refused, 403 with Retry-After. Polling is never refused.
decisions.tradeoff: How approval guessing is bounded, and who an honest viewer can be locked out by. A per-address bound lets one device behind a household's NAT stop every account there approving for 15 minutes, and it exists only where proxies are declared. A per-account bound shares nothing across accounts.
decisions.entry: Option A: failed approvals are bounded per approving account only. 10 failures in any 15 minutes, then approvals by that account are refused for 15 minutes with 403 and Retry-After, the numbers of D-020's known-device bound, which are right here. The guesser is signed in, so the account is the identity; an address adds only collateral lockout. A refusal checks no code, counts toward nothing and does not lengthen itself. It touches nothing else of the account: its tokens, playback and password sign-in go on. Connect polling and redemption are never refused. The bound holds across replicas and restarts. Each refusal is logged with the account's name and counted in a metric, so the operator sees who is guessing. docs/access.md states the 960 guesses a day per account and what a hit gives. Given up: accounts share no bound, so several colluding accounts multiply the guesses. Rejected: B and C (a household locked out by one device, and Quick Connect is D-020's way around a password lockout); D (codes guessable without limit).
decisions.serves: PRODUCT.md: 'Signing in is easy and safe. A password, a code entered on the TV from a phone'; 'Nothing is hidden… every failure is reported with its reason, never silent'; 'Installing is boring'.

decisions.brief: Quick Connect: Initiate is anonymous, so live codes can be flooded. Options: (A) a fixed maximum of live codes, refusing new Initiate past it; (B) evict the oldest live code; (C) per-address Initiate caps beside a global cap, needing trustedProxies; (D) no cap.
decisions.tradeoff: Under a flood, either a new TV cannot start Quick Connect until codes expire (A), or a TV already showing a code has it silently stop working (B). With no cap, live codes fill the 6-digit space, so a viewer's mistyped approval can sign a stranger's device into their account.
decisions.entry: Option A: at most 100 live codes across all replicas, pending or approved and unredeemed; past it Initiate is refused and no code already issued is touched, so a code a TV shows works for its full time. Not configurable. 100 is far above the devices a deployment of hundreds of viewers pairs within 10 minutes, and when full of a flooder's codes a mistyped approval lands on one about 1 time in 10,000. Each refused Initiate is logged with its reason and counted in a metric; docs/access.md and docs/running.md state the cap and that password sign-in is unaffected. The refusal's status is chosen from what jellyfin-web is observed to show for it, so that it does not read as an unreachable server. Rejected: B (an honest viewer's approval then fails as an unknown code and counts toward D-078's bound, so a flood would lock honest accounts out; the failure arrives late and unexplained); D (the mistyped-approval risk above). Backlog: C, promoted when the metric shows the cap reached on the dogfood or at an operator's. Given up: an anonymous flooder can keep new TVs from starting Quick Connect while the flood lasts, and together with name guessing (D-020) can keep a viewer on a new device out; known devices and password sign-in still work.
